content.text: Electricity is generated at power stations, but consumers are often hundreds of kilometres away. How do we get electricity from power stations to homes and businesses efficiently? The National Grid is an engineering marvel that uses transformers and high-voltage transmission to minimise energy losses.

The National Grid transmits electricity at high voltage (up to 400 kV) to reduce energy losses. Since P = I squared R, reducing the current by increasing the voltage dramatically cuts the power wasted as heat in the transmission cables.
is the network of cables, pylons, and transformers that distributes electricity across the country.

A very common exam question asks you to explain why high voltage reduces energy losses. Structure your answer in three steps: (1) for the same power, higher voltage means lower current (P = IV), (2) power lost in cables depends on current squared (P = I squared R), (3) therefore lower current means much less energy wasted as heat.

"Higher voltage is more dangerous, so we should use low voltage"
— High voltage is used in insulated cables on tall pylons, away from people. The efficiency gains are essential.
— The grid is a distribution network, not storage. Electricity flows instantly from generation to consumption.
— Transmission is at 275 kV or 400 kV. Multiple step-down transformers reduce it to 230 V.
"Thick cables mean less resistance, so voltage doesn't matter"
— Even thick cables have resistance. High voltage is still essential for efficiency.
— They're 10-20× more expensive. Overhead lines are used where practical.

The National Grid needs transformers at both ends: step-up transformers at the power station (to increase voltage for efficient transmission) and step-down transformers at substations (to reduce voltage to 230 V for safe domestic use). This is why AC is used -- transformers only work with AC.

High voltage means low current for the same power (P = IV). Power loss in cables = I²R, so reducing the current dramatically reduces wasted energy. Transmitting at 230 V would require enormous currents and most energy would be lost as heat.
— Four times the generated power; completely impractical. b)

Step-up transformers at the power station increase the voltage (e.g. 25 kV to 400 kV), reducing the current for efficient long-distance transmission. Step-down transformers at substations progressively reduce the voltage (to 33 kV, then 11 kV, then 230 V) for safe distribution to consumers.

Transformers only work with AC because they rely on a changing magnetic field to induce a voltage in the secondary coil. DC produces a constant field with no change in flux, so no voltage is induced. Without transformers, voltage cannot be efficiently stepped up or down for transmission.
The power loss would decrease by a factor of 4.
— P_loss = I²R; halving I gives (I/2)² = I²/4, so losses are quartered. The I² relationship means power loss is very sensitive to current changes. (reasoning)

Overhead lines: cheaper to install (10-20x less expensive), easier to maintain and repair, naturally air-cooled; but visual impact on landscape, safety risk, and vulnerable to weather damage. Underground cables: no visual impact, weather-protected, safer for public; but much more expensive, harder to locate and repair faults, and may overheat without natural cooling.
